title: The Deliverance, the search
hookLine: al-Ghazali describes his thirst to know things as they really are (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal)
tomorrow: what if the answer can't be reached by thinking harder?

cards: The application has a box, and the box has a question: what are you searching for? The cursor blinks. The safe answers line up: a career, a city, a cause.
Underneath them sits the real one, the one you'd never type. Do I actually believe what I was raised to believe, or did I just inherit it? Where do you start with a question like that?
A scholar named al-Ghazali started by writing it down, in a short book that tells the story of his own search: al-Munqidh min al-Dalal, The Deliverance from Error.

teach.b: He opens with something like a confession. From his early years, he writes, he had a thirst to grasp the real nature of things, and he says it wasn't his choice: it was placed in him by God, part of how he was made.
Then he names the exact question in that blinking box. He noticed that children tend to grow up holding whatever their parents hold, in every community, his own included. He didn't mock that.

He asked what it would mean to know for himself, and not only by imitation, the word for which is taqlid. So he set the bar very high. He wanted certain knowledge, knowledge so clear it leaves no room for doubt at all.
And he went looking: through the theologians, the philosophers, the teachers who claimed hidden knowledge, the Sufis, testing each one. Here's what's surprising about this book.
It's written by a man already well-known for his learning, looking back, and he doesn't hide that the search broke him for a while.
Today's point is smaller and braver.
In this tradition, a thirst for truth isn't treated as a threat to faith. Al-Ghazali presents it as a gift, a drive God placed in him. The questioning wasn't the opposite of his faith.
It was the road he walked to find it.

how: Muslims read al-Ghazali's Deliverance from Error as the story of his own search; some teachers give it to students wrestling with doubt, or with the difference between inherited and examined faith.

games.q: your younger cousin whispers that she's not sure she believes, she just goes along. she's scared to say it. what fits al-Ghazali's book best?
o: tell her not to think about it; questions only lead people away.
tell her that wanting to know for herself is a thirst worth honoring.
tell her she clearly doesn't believe, so she should stop pretending.
games.why: al-Ghazali called his own thirst for truth a gift from God, and he moved from inherited belief toward knowing for himself.

practice: On paper, finish this sentence by hand, as honestly as you can: what I really seek is. Don't polish it. Then, for the sit, read your line once and let it be a real question, not a test you can fail.
